clue.text: Lamb's tail is attached to a 'larger beast

indicators.note: a word's tail is its final letter, so only the end of Lamb's is wanted

parts.note: something attached to a thing is on it

explanation.surface: A lamb's tail is fixed onto a bigger animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tail' takes B, the last letter of 'Lamb's'; IS is given as written; 'attached to' gives ON.
explanation.definitionFit: The bison is a big wild ox, much larger than a lamb.

clue.text: Musicians: sworn to penury up north, we hear.?

indicators.note: what we hear is the sound of a phrase, not its spelling

parts.note: in northern English brass means money, so someone sworn to poverty has brass banned

explanation.surface: Musicians who have taken a vow of poverty in the north of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass is northern English slang for money; 'brass banned' (money forbidden) sounds like the name for a group of cornet and tuba players, a Northern tradition.
explanation.definitionFit: A band of brass instrument players is a group of performers.

clue.text: Jumbly riddle

explanation.surface: A muddled puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: In Edward Lear's poem The Jumblies, the Jumblies went to sea in one; a riddle is also a coarse kind of strainer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lear's Jumblies sailed in a mesh vessel, and a riddle is a coarse sifting device.

clue.text: Writing, one has -to write up" Jobs for the. Boys scandal

indicators.note: in a down clue reading up means the whole string is taken from bottom to top

parts.note: MS is a manuscript, a piece of writing
the Roman numeral I is one
to pen something is to write it

explanation.surface: A written report exposes a scandal of jobs for friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is a link; 'up' reverses the whole run MS-I-TO-PEN, giving the answer in a down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Favouritism in handing out posts to relatives and cronies is the classic jobs-for-the-boys wrong.

clue.text: Poor prisoner's short cut to acquittal ?"

definitions.text: Poor prisoner's short cut to acquittal ?

parts.words: Poor prisoner's short cut to acquittal
parts.note: an old cheap arrangement under which a prisoner standing trial could pick any barrister present in court for a small fee

explanation.surface: A penniless convict looks for a quick way to be found not guilty.
explanation.walkthrough: In English courts a prisoner could hand a barrister in court a nominal fee from the dock and be defended without a solicitor; 'short' hints at the brevity of that brief.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a legal instruction given straight from the dock to counsel, a cheap route to a defence.

clue.text: The same earth 'goddess who married the sea

parts.note: do, short for ditto, means the same
Ge or Gaea is the Greek goddess of the earth

explanation.surface: An earth goddess who wed the ocean too.
explanation.walkthrough: Each year the chief magistrate of Venice threw a ring into the Adriatic to marry the city to the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The ruler of Venice performed an annual ceremony wedding the city to the Adriatic.

clue.text: Wild-cats one confined to college-so punished

indicators.note: wild means out of order, so the letters of cats are rearranged

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
a student who is gated is kept within college as a punishment

explanation.surface: Feral cats, one of them kept indoors at college, are therefore disciplined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' turns CATS into CAST; then I and GATED. 'so' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To castigate is to scold or punish severely.

clue.text: Warrior'queen loses two articles of clothing

indicators.note: losing things means taking them out

parts.note: Boadicea was the warrior queen of the Iceni who fought the Romans in Britain
a is the indefinite article, so two articles are two As

explanation.surface: A warrior queen sheds two pieces of her armour.
explanation.walkthrough: BOADICEA loses its two As (the second and last letters) to leave the answer. 'of' is a link. Boadicea led a British revolt against Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodice is the close-fitting upper part of a dress, a garment.

clue.text: Beginning with, nice point to unravel

indicators.note: something unravelled is undone and loose, so the letters of nice point are rearranged

explanation.surface: Starting with a fine point that comes undone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to unravel' signals rearranging NICE POINT; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An inception is the start or founding of something.

clue.text: Stuff once seen 'at the Aldwych

explanation.surface: Material that used to be on stage at a London theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: Farce is forcemeat stuffing; the Aldwych is a London theatre famous in the 1920s for the farces of Ben Travers.
explanation.definitionFit: Forcemeat is a stuffing, and the Aldwych theatre was known for broad comedies.

clue.text: Are going to work without the Attorney General in court

indicators.note: here without means outside, so the work sits around the lawyer's abbreviation

parts.note: an opus is a work, especially a musical composition
AG is the abbreviation for Attorney General

explanation.surface: Going to work without the government's chief lawyer in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense 'outside', so the work wraps the lawyer's letters; 'going to' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Areopagus was the ancient Athenian council and law court on the hill of Ares.

clue.text: Russian backing includes care of, stage design

indicators.note: one piece includes another, so it is placed around it
backing means going backwards, so the word for the Russian is read right to left

parts.note: Red was a common label for a Soviet Russian
c/o, CO, is the postal abbreviation for care of

explanation.surface: Russian sponsorship covers the cost of looking after a theatrical set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns RED into DER, which 'includes' CO to give DE-CO-R.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre decor is the scenery and furnishing that make up the look of a stage set.

clue.text: Seat is adjustable as day bed for this?

indicators.note: something adjustable can be rearranged, so the letters of seat is are shuffled

explanation.surface: A seat that adjusts serves as a daybed for an afternoon rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adjustable' rearranges SEAT IS; the definition is a pointer: a day bed is the thing you use for this nap.
explanation.definitionFit: A siesta is a short afternoon sleep, the kind of rest a daybed is made for.

clue.text: Record. pile improperly made by diabolical Shavian

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record

indicators.note: done improperly means arranged wrongly, so the letters of pile are mixed

explanation.surface: A record heap badly made by a devilish follower of George Bernard Shaw.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw wrote the play The Devil's Disciple, so 'diabolical Shavian' points to its title character; 'made by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Shaw's play The Devil's Disciple is a follower of the Devil.

clue.text: South Africa's Roundhead Club

parts.note: reads as a society of Cromwell's supporters, but means a heavy stick with a round end used in South Africa

explanation.surface: A South African society for Cromwell's Parliamentarians.
explanation.walkthrough: Roundheads were Cromwell's side in the English Civil War; here 'round head' is a knob, and the club is a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a short wooden stick with a heavy rounded top, used as a weapon by southern African peoples.

clue.text: This maid sang of Mount Abora (Coleridge).

definitions.text: This maid sang of Mount Abora (Coleridge).

parts.words: This maid sang of Mount Abora (Coleridge).
parts.note: points to Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan, where a maid with a dulcimer sings of Mount Abora

explanation.surface: A quotation question about a singing girl in a Coleridge poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Kubla Khan has the lines 'It was an Abyssinian maid, / And on her dulcimer she played, / Singing of Mount Abora.'
explanation.definitionFit: The poem describes the singer as a maid from Ethiopia, the old Abyssinia.

clue.text: "Grey ?""Not us !" says one in agitation

indicators.note: agitated things are stirred up, so the letters of grey not us are mixed

explanation.surface: A young person protests that grey hair is not for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in agitation' rearranges GREY NOT US; the 'one' saying 'Not us!' to grey hair is a young person. 'says' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A juvenile is the kind of person who would deny going grey.

clue.text: Salute ten in' Rome

explanation.surface: Greeting ten people in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: Ten in Roman numerals is X, which is also the sign written for a kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiss is an affectionate greeting, and an X, the Roman ten, is how a kiss is written in letters.

clue.text: Samsonian clue for honey

parts.note: Samson's riddle in Judges, 'Out of the strong came forth', describes honey found in a lion's carcass

explanation.surface: A riddle Samson set whose answer was honey.
explanation.walkthrough: Samson's riddle was 'Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth' this; the answer was honey in the lion.
explanation.definitionFit: In Samson's riddle, honey is described by its sugary quality coming out of the strong lion.

clue.text: Hitler's. feudal superior?

parts.note: a lord above other lords in the feudal system, and the Allied codename for the D-Day landings, Hitler's defeat

explanation.surface: Was there a feudal lord above Hitler?
explanation.walkthrough: In feudalism the lord above vassals has this title; it was also the codename of the 1944 Normandy invasion that sealed Hitler's fate.
explanation.definitionFit: A feudal lord with authority over lesser lords is a supreme ruler; the Allied invasion took the same name.

clue.text: Party went with a bang?

explanation.surface: Did the party go off with a bang?
explanation.walkthrough: A drum was an old word for a large evening party; a drum also makes a bang when struck.
explanation.definitionFit: Drum once meant a fashionable gathering, and the instrument is something that produces bangs.

clue.text: Keeping even cobras can be tricky

indicators.note: snakes that can be tricky are hard to handle, so their letters, with even, are moved around

explanation.surface: Looking after even cobras can be awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be tricky' signals rearranging EVEN COBRAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Observance is the keeping of a rule, custom or festival.

clue.text: No new measures to make sports grounds

explanation.surface: Without new policies, build arenas.
explanation.walkthrough: Stadia are ancient Greek measures of length, about 185 metres, so not new; it is also a plural of stadium. 'to make' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek stadion was an old unit of distance, and the plural also means arenas for games.

clue.text: Got back to the upper air, but not solo

indicators.note: read back, so the letters of got go right to left

parts.note: ether was the old name for the clear upper air

explanation.surface: Someone came back to the surface air, but with company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link. Ether is the old poetic name for the clear sky above the clouds.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something along with others rather than alone is doing it jointly.

clue.text: It's characteristic that gold would make a turncoat

indicators.note: the answer and gold would together make the turncoat, so gold is taken from it

parts.note: a turncoat is a traitor who changes sides
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: It's typical that wealth turns a man into a defector.
explanation.walkthrough: TRAITOR is the answer plus OR, gold in heraldry; take OR away to leave the answer. 'that' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A trait is a distinguishing feature or quality.

clue.text: First aid for one drying up when he .: :

definitions.text: First aid for one drying up when he

parts.words: First aid for one drying up when he
parts.note: an actor who forgets his lines is said to dry, and the first help he gets is the next line whispered from the wings

explanation.surface: Emergency help for someone who has dried out; the clue runs on into 26.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 26, 'took part': 'drying up when he acted' means an actor forgetting his lines. 'First aid' looks medical; here it is a whispered cue.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre helper whispers the forgotten line to a stuck actor; that cue is the help.

clue.text: Trapped in London'?Find a hole in Cornwall

definitions.text: Trapped in London'?Find a hole in Cornwall

parts.words: Trapped in London'?Find a hole in Cornwall
parts.note: a small rodent is trapped in houses, and with hole added it names a Cornish fishing village

explanation.surface: Stuck in London? Go and find a cove in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: Mousehole is a fishing village in Cornwall, England's south-west tip; the rodent is the one caught in a trap in London homes.
explanation.definitionFit: A small rodent is caught in traps, and adding hole names the Cornish village Mousehole.

clue.text: An extended hand at bridge

explanation.surface: Someone's outstretched hand at a game of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at bridge' suggests the card game, but bridge is a definition in its own right. 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The width of an outstretched hand from thumb to little finger is an old measure, and an arch between supports crosses a gap.

clue.text: … took part

parts.note: played a role on stage, completing the sentence begun at 23 across

explanation.walkthrough: The dots join this to 23: 'First aid for one drying up when he ... took part'. Taking a part is playing a role on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a part in a play means performing it.

clue.text: Make copy concerning output

parts.note: re means about or concerning
produce is what is turned out, the output of a farm or factory

explanation.surface: A journalist writing material about production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make copy' suggests journalism; here it simply means duplicate.
explanation.definitionFit: To duplicate something is to make another of it.

clue.text: Two Jacks point' to an abysmal result

parts.note: a jack tar, or tar, is a sailor, and two of them are wanted
a jack tar, or tar, is a sailor, and two of them are wanted
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Two men named Jack point to a dreadful outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack and tar both mean sailor, so 'Two Jacks' gives TAR twice; 'to' and 'result' are links. 'abysmal' is the old sense 'of the abyss'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartarus was the deepest pit of the Greek underworld, so the adjective means hellish, of the bottomless abyss.

clue.text: Get in line, 'or get clobbered'!

explanation.surface: Fall into line, or you'll be hit!
explanation.walkthrough: Soldiers dress ranks by lining up; 'clobber' is British slang for clothes, so 'get clobbered' is get clothed.
explanation.definitionFit: On parade, troops align themselves in ranks; and putting on garments is clothing oneself.
